description: Reptiles, dinosaurs, pterosaurs, Mesozoic sea reptiles and birds: everything descended from the first sauropsids, from Hylonomus to the chicken. All of it hangs from the backbone node 'sauropsida'.

nodes.name: Hylonomus
nodes.summary: One of the oldest known reptiles: a small, lizard-shaped insect-eater about 20 cm long that scurried through Carboniferous coal forests more than 310 million years ago.
facts: Its skeletons were found inside the fossilised hollow stumps of giant club-moss trees at Joggins, Nova Scotia.
It looked like a lizard but was not one; lizards would not appear for another 70 million years or more.

nodes.name: Diapsids
nodes.summary: Reptiles with two openings in the skull behind each eye, which gave jaw muscles room to bulge. Lizards, snakes, crocodiles, dinosaurs and birds are all diapsids.
facts: One of the earliest known diapsids, Petrolacosaurus, was a 40 cm lizard-like animal from Kansas about 302 million years ago.
Turtles lost their skull openings, but DNA shows they are diapsids too.

nodes.name: Ichthyosaurs
nodes.summary: "Fish lizards": sea reptiles shaped like dolphins, with paddles, a tail fin and a back fin. They ruled the oceans for over 150 million years, but nobody is sure exactly which land reptiles they came from.
facts: Fossils of mothers caught in the act of giving birth show ichthyosaurs had live babies at sea, tail first like dolphins.
Mary Anning and her brother found the first ichthyosaur skeleton recognised by science on the cliffs of Lyme Regis around 1811–1812, when she was about 12.
The biggest, like Shonisaurus, were more than 15 metres long, close to the size of a sperm whale.

nodes.name: Ophthalmosaurus
nodes.summary: A sleek, 4-metre Jurassic ichthyosaur with gigantic eyes, probably used to hunt squid-like prey in the dim depths.
facts: Its eyes were about 22 cm across, among the largest relative to body size of any vertebrate.
Bony rings inside its eyes helped them withstand water pressure on deep dives.

nodes.name: Sauropterygians
nodes.summary: A great family of Mesozoic sea reptiles, from shell-crushing placodonts and long-necked nothosaurs to the plesiosaurs. Their exact place on the reptile tree is still debated.
facts: They were not dinosaurs, even though they lived at the same time.
Their ancestors walked on land and gradually turned their legs into flippers.

nodes.name: Plesiosaurs
nodes.summary: Sea reptiles that "flew" through the water with four big flippers. Some had tiny heads on enormously long necks; others, the pliosaurs, had huge heads and short necks.
facts: A 2011 fossil of a pregnant Polycotylus showed plesiosaurs gave birth to a single large baby, which mothers may have cared for.
Mary Anning found the first nearly complete plesiosaur skeleton in 1823.
Many 'Loch Ness Monster' stories imagine a plesiosaur, but they died out 66 million years ago.

nodes.name: Elasmosaurus
nodes.summary: A plesiosaur with one of the longest necks of any animal ever: about 7 metres of neck on a 10-metre body, swimming in the shallow sea that once split North America in two.
facts: Its neck had 72 vertebrae; yours has 7.
In 1868 Edward Drinker Cope put its head on the end of its tail by mistake, and his rival Othniel Marsh made sure everyone heard about it, kicking off the 'Bone Wars'.

nodes.name: Liopleurodon
nodes.summary: A short-necked pliosaur with a crocodile-like head full of big conical teeth, the top predator of Jurassic European seas.
facts: TV once showed it as 25 metres long, but the real animal was about 6–7 metres. Still bigger than a great white shark.
Its nostrils may have let it 'smell' the water as it swam, to track prey.

nodes.name: Lepidosaurs
nodes.summary: Scaly reptiles that shed their skin: the tuatara plus all lizards and snakes. With over 11,000 species, it is the most successful reptile group alive.
facts: Many lepidosaurs can drop their tail to escape a predator and grow a new one.
The oldest known member, Megachirella, lived about 244 million years ago in the Italian Alps.

nodes.name: Rhynchocephalians
nodes.summary: A once-worldwide order of lizard-like reptiles that thrived in the Triassic and Jurassic, then dwindled until only one species was left: the tuatara.
facts: Some extinct rhynchocephalians, like Pleurosaurus, became long, eel-like swimmers in the sea.

nodes.name: Tuatara
nodes.summary: A New Zealand reptile that looks like a lizard but isn't one. It is the last survivor of a lineage that split from lizards and snakes about 240 million years ago.
facts: Young tuatara have a light-sensitive 'third eye' on top of the head, which becomes covered by scales as they grow.
They stay active at temperatures as low as 5 °C, colder than almost any other reptile can bear, and can live for over 100 years.
Its teeth are not separate teeth but sharp points of the jawbone itself.

nodes.name: Lizards & snakes
nodes.summary: The squamates: lizards and snakes. Snakes are really a branch of legless lizards, and together they make up more than 11,000 species, more than all mammals.
facts: Their lower jaw is loosely hinged, and in snakes the two halves can even spread apart to swallow huge meals.
Legs have been lost more than 20 times in different lizard groups.

nodes.name: Geckos
nodes.summary: Wall-walking lizards with sticky-looking toes that are not sticky at all. Their feet are covered in millions of microscopic hairs that grip by tiny molecular forces.
facts: A gecko can hang from a glass ceiling by a single toe.
Most geckos have no eyelids, so they clean their eyes by licking them.
Unlike most lizards, geckos chirp and bark; the name 'gecko' copies the call of one species.

nodes.name: Green iguana
nodes.summary: A big plant-eating lizard of Central and South American rainforests, up to 1.7 m long including its whip-like tail.
facts: It has a pale 'third eye' on top of its head that senses light and shadows, a warning of birds swooping from above.
Iguanas can drop 12–15 metres from a tree onto the ground and walk away unhurt.

nodes.name: Chameleons
nodes.summary: Slow-moving tree lizards with turret eyes, grasping feet and a ballistic tongue. Most of the world's species live in Africa and Madagascar.
facts: Each eye moves on its own, so a chameleon can look forwards and backwards at the same time.
They change colour by tuning a lattice of tiny crystals in their skin, which changes how light reflects.
Some can shoot their tongue out to twice their body length in a fraction of a second.

nodes.name: Komodo dragon
nodes.summary: The largest living lizard, up to 3 metres long and 70 kg. This monitor lizard ambushes deer and water buffalo on a few Indonesian islands.
facts: Its lower jaw has venom glands that stop blood from clotting.
Females can lay fertile eggs without ever meeting a male (parthenogenesis).
Its teeth have edges coated in iron, which keeps them sharp.

nodes.name: Mosasaurs
nodes.summary: Giant sea-going lizards that ruled Late Cretaceous oceans after the ichthyosaurs vanished. They were close relatives of monitor lizards, or perhaps of snakes; scientists still argue which.
facts: Like whales, mosasaurs gave birth to live young at sea.
Some had a shark-like, crescent-shaped tail fin.

nodes.name: Mosasaurus
nodes.summary: The "lizard of the Meuse": a sea monster up to about 12 metres long with a double-hinged jaw and a second row of teeth on the roof of its mouth.
facts: Its giant skull, dug out of a chalk quarry near Maastricht in the 18th century, was one of the first fossils to make people realise species could go extinct.
In 1795 French soldiers seized the famous skull as a prize of war. It is still in Paris today.

nodes.name: Snakes
nodes.summary: Legless lizards that turned a long body into a winning design. About 4,000 species squeeze, bite or inject venom, and they live everywhere except Antarctica and a few islands.
facts: Early snakes such as Najash, from 95 million years ago, still had small back legs.
A snake 'smells' with its forked tongue, flicking scent particles to an organ in the roof of its mouth.
A snake can have more than 200 pairs of ribs.

nodes.name: Pythons
nodes.summary: Non-venomous constrictors of Africa, Asia and Australia that kill by squeezing. The reticulated python is the longest snake alive, sometimes over 6 metres.
facts: Pythons still have tiny claw-like spurs, the remains of hind legs.
After a huge meal, a Burmese python's heart can grow about 40% bigger to help digest it.
Escaped pet Burmese pythons have spread through Florida's Everglades.

nodes.name: Titanoboa
nodes.summary: The largest snake ever found: a boa relative around 13 metres long and over a tonne, which lived in steamy rainforests just 6 million years after the dinosaurs died.
facts: Its fossils were found in the Cerrejón coal mine in Colombia.
It was probably as long as a school bus and as heavy as a small car.
It probably spent much of its time in rivers, hunting fish and crocodile relatives.

nodes.name: King cobra
nodes.summary: The world's longest venomous snake, reaching over 5 metres. It lives in Asian forests and mostly eats other snakes.
facts: Its scientific name Ophiophagus means 'snake-eater'.
It is the only snake known to build a nest of leaves for its eggs, and the female guards it.
Despite the name, it is not a 'true' cobra (genus Naja), and in 2024 scientists split it into four separate species.

nodes.name: Rattlesnakes
nodes.summary: Venomous pit vipers of the Americas that warn intruders with a buzzing rattle on the tail.
facts: The rattle is made of keratin, like your fingernails. A new segment is added every time the snake sheds its skin.
Heat-sensing pits between eyes and nostrils let rattlesnakes 'see' warm-blooded prey in total darkness.
They can shake the rattle around 50–90 times a second.

nodes.name: Turtles + archosaurs
nodes.summary: A surprise revealed by DNA: turtles are more closely related to crocodiles, dinosaurs and birds than they are to lizards and snakes.
facts: So a tortoise is a closer cousin of a chicken than of an iguana.

nodes.name: Turtles
nodes.summary: Reptiles that carry their house on their back. Their shell is built from widened ribs and backbone fused to bony plates, so a turtle can never climb out of it.
facts: About 360 species of turtles and tortoises live today.
Turtle ancestors may first have evolved broad ribs for digging, not for armour.

nodes.name: Odontochelys
nodes.summary: A Triassic "half-shelled turtle with teeth" from China. It had a complete belly shell but only widened ribs on its back: evolution caught halfway.
facts: Modern turtles have toothless beaks; Odontochelys still had teeth.
It lived in shallow coastal waters about 220 million years ago.

nodes.name: Sea turtles
nodes.summary: Turtles with flippers that cross whole oceans. Females haul themselves onto the same beaches where they hatched to bury their eggs.
facts: Hatchlings use Earth's magnetic field like a built-in map.
The temperature of the sand decides whether eggs hatch as males or females: warmer nests make more females.
The leatherback, the largest living turtle, can dive over 1,000 metres deep and lives almost entirely on jellyfish.

nodes.name: Archelon
nodes.summary: The largest turtle ever found: about 4.6 metres long, with a leathery shell, paddling the Cretaceous seas over what is now South Dakota.
facts: Its closest living relative may be the leatherback sea turtle.
The best skeleton is missing a back flipper, possibly bitten off by a mosasaur or shark.

nodes.name: Tortoises
nodes.summary: Land-living turtles with domed shells and elephant-like legs. Several have floated across seas and grown into giants on remote islands.
facts: Tortoises are among the longest-lived animals: some have passed 150 years.

nodes.name: Galápagos giant tortoise
nodes.summary: Giant tortoises weighing over 250 kg whose ancestors drifted from South America to the Galápagos Islands. Each island evolved its own shell shape, which helped inspire Darwin.
facts: The islands were named after them: 'galápago' is an old Spanish word for tortoise.
Sailors once stacked them alive in ships' holds because they could survive for months without food or water.
Lonesome George, the last tortoise from Pinta Island, died in 2012.

nodes.name: Archosaurs
nodes.summary: The "ruling reptiles": the group containing crocodiles on one branch and pterosaurs, dinosaurs and birds on the other. They rose to power after the great Permian extinction.
facts: Crocodiles and birds are each other's closest living relatives.
Like birds, crocodiles have a four-chambered heart and air flowing one way through their lungs.

nodes.name: Crocodile line
nodes.summary: The crocodile branch of the archosaurs. In the Triassic it was far more varied than the dinosaurs, with armoured plant-eaters, huge predators and even fast two-legged runners.
facts: Some Triassic crocodile relatives, like Effigia, walked on two legs and had toothless beaks, looking just like ostrich dinosaurs.
Most of the crocodile line died out in the end-Triassic extinction about 201 million years ago, which helped dinosaurs take over.

nodes.name: Postosuchus
nodes.summary: A 4–5 metre predator of the Late Triassic with a deep skull and dagger teeth. It was a top predator in a world where dinosaurs were still small.
facts: It is not a dinosaur: it is closer to today's crocodiles.
It is named after the town of Post, Texas, near where it was found.

nodes.name: Crocodylomorphs
nodes.summary: Crocodiles and all their extinct relatives. The first ones were small, slender, long-legged land runners. Later ones took to rivers, the open sea and even plant-eating.
facts: Jurassic thalattosuchians were 'sea crocodiles' with flippers and a fish-like tail fin.
Crocodylomorphs survived both the end-Triassic extinction and the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs.

nodes.name: Sarcosuchus
nodes.summary: "SuperCroc": a crocodile relative around 9 metres long and up to 8 tonnes that lurked in Cretaceous rivers of what is now the Sahara Desert.
facts: Its snout ended in a strange bony bulb whose purpose is still a mystery.
Its bony back armour plates show growth rings, which suggest it kept growing for most of its 50-60 years.

nodes.name: Crocodilians
nodes.summary: Crocodiles, alligators, caimans and gharials: armoured ambush hunters that survived the asteroid which wiped out their dinosaur cousins.
facts: Crocodilians can go months without eating.
Mothers gently carry their hatchlings to the water in their jaws.
Their body plan has barely changed in tens of millions of years because it works so well.

nodes.name: Deinosuchus
nodes.summary: The "terrible crocodile": a giant alligator relative, perhaps 10 metres long, that ambushed dinosaurs at the water's edge in North America.
facts: Dinosaur bones have been found with Deinosuchus tooth marks, including those of a tyrannosaur.
Despite its size it was closer to alligators than to crocodiles.

nodes.name: American alligator
nodes.summary: A broad-snouted crocodilian of the swamps of the south-eastern USA. Once nearly hunted out, it has made a huge comeback.
facts: An alligator can grow about 3,000 teeth in its lifetime, replacing them as they wear out.
In freezing weather alligators poke their snouts up through the ice so they can keep breathing.

nodes.name: Saltwater crocodile
nodes.summary: The largest living reptile: males can exceed 6 metres and 1,000 kg. It lives from India to northern Australia and can swim far out to sea.
facts: It has the strongest bite ever measured in a living animal.
They ride ocean currents to travel between islands hundreds of kilometres apart.

nodes.name: Gharial
nodes.summary: A fish-catching crocodilian from Indian and Nepali rivers, with a long, very thin snout lined with over 100 sharp teeth. It is critically endangered.
facts: Adult males grow a bulbous knob on the snout tip called a 'ghara', after an Indian clay pot, which they use to make buzzing sounds.
Its legs are so weak that it can barely walk on land.

nodes.name: Bird-line archosaurs
nodes.summary: The branch of archosaurs leading to pterosaurs, dinosaurs and birds. Its members stood tall with their legs tucked under the body, built for speed.
facts: One of the earliest known members, Teleocrater, still walked on four legs and had crocodile-like ankles.

nodes.name: Pterosaurs
nodes.summary: The first vertebrates to fly by flapping, about 80 million years before birds. Their wings were skin stretched from an enormously long fourth finger to the legs.
facts: Pterosaurs were not dinosaurs; they were close cousins.
Many were covered in fuzzy hair-like 'pycnofibres', so some probably looked furry.
They ranged from sparrow-sized to giants as tall as a giraffe.

nodes.name: Rhamphorhynchus
nodes.summary: A long-tailed Jurassic pterosaur with forward-pointing needle teeth for snatching fish, and a diamond-shaped vane at the tip of its tail.
facts: Some fossils from Solnhofen, Germany, still have fish in their throats.
One specimen was found tangled in the jaws of a large fish that may have grabbed it as it skimmed the water.

nodes.name: Pterodactylus
nodes.summary: A short-tailed pterosaur with a wingspan of about a metre, and the first pterosaur ever described by scientists. 'Pterodactyl' is now used loosely for all pterosaurs.
facts: When it was first described in 1784, the naturalist Cosimo Collini wondered if it might be a sea creature using its wings as flippers.
Its fossils come from the same Bavarian limestone as Archaeopteryx.

nodes.name: Pteranodon
nodes.summary: A large, toothless pterosaur that soared over the Cretaceous inland sea of North America like a giant albatross, with a long backward-pointing head crest.
facts: Its name means 'toothless wing'.
Males had much bigger crests than females, probably for showing off.
Adult males had wingspans of over 5 metres.

nodes.name: Quetzalcoatlus
nodes.summary: One of the largest flying animals ever, with a wingspan of about 10–11 metres. Standing on the ground it was as tall as a giraffe.
facts: It probably stalked small animals on foot like a giant stork, and only flew to travel.
To take off, it likely vaulted into the air using its powerful arms.
It is named after Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent god of the Aztecs.

nodes.name: Dinosauromorphs
nodes.summary: Dinosaurs and their closest forerunners: small, slender, fast-running reptiles of the Middle Triassic.

nodes.name: Marasuchus
nodes.summary: A small Triassic sprinter from Argentina, about 40 cm long, with long hind legs. It was not quite a dinosaur, but it shows what the dinosaurs' ancestors looked like.
facts: Some scientists think Marasuchus is really the same animal as Lagosuchus, the 'rabbit crocodile'.
It weighed perhaps a few hundred grams.

nodes.name: Dinosaurs
nodes.summary: The "terrible lizards": archosaurs with legs held straight under the body and a hole right through the hip socket. Starting small in the Triassic, they dominated land for 165 million years, and they are still here as birds.
facts: The word 'dinosaur' was coined by Richard Owen in 1842.
Over 1,000 species of non-avian dinosaurs have been named, and new ones are described almost every week.
Birds are dinosaurs, so there are about 11,000 dinosaur species alive today.

nodes.name: Bird-hipped dinosaurs
nodes.summary: Plant-eating dinosaurs with a bird-like hip and an extra beak bone at the tip of the lower jaw. They include armoured, horned, dome-headed and duck-billed dinosaurs.
facts: Confusingly, birds did not come from the 'bird-hipped' dinosaurs. They evolved from the 'lizard-hipped' theropods.
Some ornithischians had hundreds of teeth packed into grinding batteries, better chewers than almost any reptile.

nodes.name: Heterodontosaurus
nodes.summary: A turkey-sized early ornithischian from South Africa with three different kinds of teeth, including tusk-like fangs.
facts: Its name means 'different-toothed lizard'. Most reptiles have teeth that all look the same.
A close relative, Tianyulong, had long bristles on its back, so these plant-eaters may have been fuzzy.

nodes.name: Armoured dinosaurs
nodes.summary: The "shield bearers": dinosaurs covered in bony plates, spikes and studs. They range from small two-legged Scutellosaurus to the tank-like ankylosaurs.

nodes.name: Stegosaurs
nodes.summary: Four-legged plant-eaters with rows of plates or spikes along the back and a spiked tail, found in North America, Europe, Africa and Asia.
facts: Africa's Kentrosaurus had spikes sticking out from its shoulders as well as its tail.

nodes.name: Stegosaurus
nodes.summary: The famous plated dinosaur: a 9-metre plant-eater with two rows of tall bony plates and four tail spikes.
facts: Tyrannosaurus lived closer in time to you than to Stegosaurus.
The tail spikes are nicknamed the 'thagomizer' after a 1982 Far Side cartoon, and real palaeontologists now use the word.
An Allosaurus backbone has been found with a hole that matches a Stegosaurus tail spike.

nodes.name: Ankylosaurs
nodes.summary: Living tanks: low, wide plant-eaters covered in bony armour, some with shoulder spikes, others with heavy tail clubs.
facts: Some even had bony eyelids.
Borealopelta, a nodosaur from Canada, is so well preserved that it looks like a statue. Pigments show it was reddish-brown on top and paler below.

nodes.name: Ankylosaurus
nodes.summary: The biggest ankylosaur, 6–8 metres long, with a bony tail club that could have broken the leg of an attacking tyrannosaur.
facts: It lived side by side with Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops until the very end of the dinosaur age.
Its name means 'fused lizard', because many of its bones and armour plates were fused together.

nodes.name: Fringe-headed dinosaurs
nodes.summary: Plant-eaters with a bony shelf at the back of the skull, which grew into the thick domes of the bone-heads and the frills of the horned dinosaurs.

nodes.name: Pachycephalosaurus
nodes.summary: The "thick-headed lizard": a two-legged plant-eater with a domed skull roof up to 25 cm thick, ringed with bony knobs.
facts: Whether bone-heads really butted heads is debated, but some domes show healed injuries that look like battle scars.
The spiky Dracorex and Stygimoloch may simply be young Pachycephalosaurus that hadn't grown their full domes yet.

nodes.name: Horned dinosaurs
nodes.summary: Beaked plant-eaters that began as small two-legged runners in Jurassic China and ended as rhino-like giants with horns and huge frills.
facts: Psittacosaurus, an early ceratopsian, had quill-like bristles on its tail, and its fossil skin shows it was dark on top and pale below for camouflage.
All ceratopsians had a parrot-like beak with a special bone on the upper jaw.

nodes.name: Protoceratops
nodes.summary: A sheep-sized horned dinosaur with a frill but no real horns, common in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia.
facts: The 'Fighting Dinosaurs' fossil shows a Protoceratops and a Velociraptor locked in combat, probably buried by a collapsing sand dune.
Its eggs had soft, leathery shells like a turtle's.
Some historians have suggested that its skulls, weathering out of the desert, inspired the legend of the griffin.

nodes.name: Triceratops
nodes.summary: The "three-horned face": a 9-metre, elephant-heavy plant-eater with two long brow horns, a nose horn and a huge bony frill. It was one of the last dinosaurs.
facts: Its skull could reach about 2.5 metres long, one of the biggest heads of any land animal ever.
Triceratops bones have been found with Tyrannosaurus bite marks, some of them healed.
It had up to 800 teeth arranged in shearing batteries.

nodes.name: Ornithopods
nodes.summary: "Bird-footed" plant-eaters that could walk on two legs or four. They became the most common large herbivores of the Late Cretaceous.
facts: They evolved a way of grinding food with their cheek teeth that worked a bit like mammal chewing, which no other reptiles had.

nodes.name: Iguanodon
nodes.summary: A 10-metre plant-eater with a spiky thumb, and the second dinosaur ever named, in 1825.
facts: The first reconstructions put its thumb spike on its nose like a rhino horn.
In 1878 coal miners in Bernissart, Belgium, found 38 Iguanodon skeletons deep underground.
It got its name because its teeth looked like giant iguana teeth.

nodes.name: Duck-billed dinosaurs
nodes.summary: The hadrosaurs: broad-beaked plant-eaters that roamed in herds across North America, Asia and Europe, many with fancy hollow crests.
facts: Their jaws held hundreds of teeth stacked in columns, constantly replaced as they wore down.
Hadrosaurus, found in New Jersey in 1858, was the first nearly complete dinosaur skeleton ever discovered.

nodes.name: Maiasaura
nodes.summary: The "good mother lizard": a duck-billed dinosaur that nested in huge colonies, where parents looked after their babies in the nest.
facts: Jack Horner found its nesting site, 'Egg Mountain' in Montana, in 1978. It was the first clear evidence that dinosaurs cared for their young.
A piece of Maiasaura bone and eggshell flew to space aboard the Space Shuttle in 1985.

nodes.name: Parasaurolophus
nodes.summary: A duck-billed dinosaur with a long, curved, hollow crest sweeping back from its head, which it likely used like a trombone.
facts: Air from its nose looped through tubes inside the crest; computer models suggest it made deep, low booming calls.
Its crest could be about a metre long.

nodes.name: Edmontosaurus
nodes.summary: A huge, crestless duck-bill up to 12 metres long, and one of Tyrannosaurus rex's main prey animals.
facts: 'Dinosaur mummies' of Edmontosaurus preserve skin, and one revealed a fleshy comb on its head like a rooster's.
One Edmontosaurus tail has a healed T. rex bite, showing it escaped a live attack.

nodes.name: Lizard-hipped dinosaurs
nodes.summary: The great branch of dinosaurs that includes the long-necked sauropods and the meat-eating theropods, and therefore birds.
facts: In 2017 some scientists proposed reshuffling the dinosaur tree so theropods sit closer to ornithischians. The debate isn't settled.

nodes.name: Herrerasaurus
nodes.summary: One of the earliest dinosaurs: a 3–6 metre two-legged predator from Argentina's 'Valley of the Moon', 231 million years ago.
facts: It is named after Victorino Herrera, a local goat herder who spotted the first skeleton in 1959.
It had a flexible joint in its lower jaw to grip struggling prey.
Scientists still argue whether it was an early theropod or an even earlier offshoot.

nodes.name: Sauropodomorphs
nodes.summary: The long-necked dinosaurs and their ancestors. They started as small two-legged omnivores and became the largest animals ever to walk the Earth.

nodes.name: Eoraptor
nodes.summary: The "dawn plunderer": a 1-metre, lightly built dinosaur from the very dawn of the dinosaur age in Argentina.
facts: It was first described as a tiny early meat-eater, but most scientists now think it was an early relative of the giant sauropods.
It had both curved, meat-ripping teeth and leaf-shaped, plant-shredding teeth.

nodes.name: Plateosaurus
nodes.summary: A 5–10 metre Triassic plant-eater from Europe that walked on its hind legs, one of the first big dinosaurs.
facts: More than 100 skeletons are known, many from animals that got stuck in mud and died.
Its wrists couldn't turn its palms downward, so it could not have walked on all fours.

nodes.name: Sauropods
nodes.summary: Giant four-legged plant-eaters with tiny heads, long necks and long tails: the biggest land animals in Earth's history.
facts: Their bones were full of air sacs connected to the lungs, just like birds', which kept their huge skeletons light.
Even the largest hatched from eggs no bigger than a grapefruit, then grew by thousands of times.
They swallowed leaves without chewing and let their giant guts do the work.

nodes.name: Diplodocids
nodes.summary: Long, low-slung sauropods with whip-like tails and peg-shaped teeth for raking plants, stars of the Late Jurassic of North America.

nodes.name: Diplodocus
nodes.summary: One of the longest dinosaurs, about 25 metres or more, mostly neck and tail.
facts: Steel tycoon Andrew Carnegie gave casts of his Diplodocus, 'Dippy', to museums around the world, which made it one of the most famous dinosaurs ever.
It replaced each tooth about once a month.

nodes.name: Apatosaurus
nodes.summary: A massive, heavy-built sauropod with a very thick neck, around 22 metres long and maybe 20 tonnes.
facts: Its name means 'deceptive lizard'.
Its unusually thick neck may have been used for shoving matches between rivals.

nodes.name: Brontosaurus
nodes.summary: The "thunder lizard": a giant Jurassic sauropod that was 'cancelled' for over a century and then brought back.
facts: In 1903 scientists decided Brontosaurus was just Apatosaurus, but in 2015 a huge study found it different enough to be its own genus again.
The famous skeleton once displayed as Brontosaurus had the wrong skull on it for decades.

nodes.name: Brachiosaurus
nodes.summary: A giraffe-shaped giant whose front legs were longer than its back legs, letting it browse treetops about 9 metres up.
facts: Its name means 'arm lizard', after those long front legs.
The famous mounted skeleton in Berlin was renamed Giraffatitan in 2009 because it turned out to be a different animal.

nodes.name: Titanosaurs
nodes.summary: The last great sauropods, which spread across every continent including Antarctica. They include the heaviest land animals ever known.
facts: Some titanosaurs had bony armour in their skin.
At Auca Mahuevo in Argentina, thousands of titanosaur eggs were found, some with fossil embryo skin inside.

nodes.name: Argentinosaurus
nodes.summary: A contender for the heaviest land animal of all time: maybe 30–35 metres long and 65–80 tonnes, about as heavy as ten elephants.
facts: A rancher found its first bone in 1987 and thought it was a log of petrified wood.
One of its back vertebrae is about as tall as a 12-year-old.

nodes.name: Patagotitan
nodes.summary: A colossal titanosaur from Patagonia, about 31–37 metres long and over 50 tonnes, known from several skeletons.
facts: A farm worker spotted the first bone poking out of the ground in 2010.
Its thigh bone is about 2.4 metres long, taller than most adults.
Its cast at the American Museum of Natural History is so long that its head pokes out of the gallery doorway.

nodes.name: Theropods
nodes.summary: The "beast-footed" dinosaurs: two-legged hunters with hollow bones, three main toes and wishbones. Almost every meat-eating dinosaur was a theropod, and so is every bird.
facts: The wishbone in your roast chicken is a theropod feature: Tyrannosaurus and Velociraptor had one too.
Theropods existed for over 230 million years, and they still do.

nodes.name: Coelophysis
nodes.summary: A slender, 3-metre Triassic hunter that may have lived in packs. It is one of the best-known early dinosaurs.
facts: At Ghost Ranch, New Mexico, hundreds of skeletons were found jumbled together.
It was long accused of cannibalism, but the 'babies' in its belly turned out to be small crocodile relatives.
A Coelophysis skull flew to the Mir space station in 1998.

nodes.name: Dilophosaurus
nodes.summary: A 7-metre Early Jurassic predator with two thin, bony crests on its head, the biggest land predator of its time in North America.
facts: The neck frill and venom-spitting in Jurassic Park are made up; there is no evidence for either.
The real animal was about twice the size of the movie version.

nodes.name: Carnotaurus
nodes.summary: The "meat-eating bull": an 8-metre abelisaur from Argentina with two thick horns above its eyes and ridiculously stubby arms.
facts: Its arms were even tinier, relative to its body, than T. rex's; its forearms were barely there.
Skin impressions show it was covered in small scales with rows of bigger bumps.
Powerful tail muscles may have made it one of the fastest big theropods.

nodes.name: Tetanurans
nodes.summary: "Stiff tails": the advanced theropods, including spinosaurs, allosaurs, tyrannosaurs, raptors and birds.

nodes.name: Megalosaurus
nodes.summary: A 6-metre Jurassic predator from England, and the very first dinosaur ever given a scientific name, by William Buckland in 1824.
facts: A bone found in 1676 was thought to be the thigh of a giant human. It was probably Megalosaurus.
Charles Dickens imagined a Megalosaurus 'waddling like an elephantine lizard' up a London street in Bleak House (1852).

nodes.name: Spinosaurus
nodes.summary: A fish-eating giant with a crocodile-like snout and a tall sail on its back, perhaps the longest predatory dinosaur at around 14 metres.
facts: The original fossils were destroyed when Munich was bombed in 1944; for decades only drawings and photos remained.
Whether it swam after its prey or waded like a giant heron is one of palaeontology's hottest arguments.

nodes.name: Allosaurs
nodes.summary: Big-headed, three-fingered predators that were the top hunters on most continents for over 70 million years, before tyrannosaurs took over in the north.

nodes.name: Allosaurus
nodes.summary: The top predator of Late Jurassic North America: 8.5 metres long, with blade-like teeth and big three-fingered claws.
facts: A skeleton nicknamed 'Big Al' had 19 injuries and infections, a tough life on the Jurassic floodplains.
It may have attacked by slamming its open jaws down like a hatchet.

nodes.name: Giganotosaurus
nodes.summary: A South American giant of 12–13 metres, about as long as T. rex but lighter, with thin, blade-like teeth for slicing flesh.
facts: Amateur fossil hunter Rubén Carolini found it in 1993 while driving a dune buggy in Patagonia.
It may have hunted giant titanosaurs, perhaps in groups.

nodes.name: Coelurosaurs
nodes.summary: The feathered branch of theropods, from tiny Compsognathus to Tyrannosaurus, the raptors and birds.
facts: Fossils from China show that many, perhaps most, coelurosaurs were covered in feathers.

nodes.name: Tyrannosaurs
nodes.summary: The tyrant lizards began as small, crested, feathered hunters in the Jurassic, and only became giants in the last 20 million years of the dinosaur age.
facts: One of the earliest relatives, Proceratosaurus, lived in Jurassic England.
Early Guanlong was only about 3 metres long and had a flashy crest on its snout.

nodes.name: Yutyrannus
nodes.summary: The "beautiful feathered tyrant": a 9-metre tyrannosaur relative from China, covered in long shaggy feathers.
facts: It is the largest animal known with direct fossil evidence of feathers.
Its feathers were up to 20 cm long, perhaps to keep it warm in a chilly climate.

nodes.name: Tyrannosaurus rex
nodes.summary: The tyrant lizard king: a 12-metre, 8-tonne predator with bone-crushing jaws and forward-facing eyes. It was one of the last non-avian dinosaurs, alive when the asteroid struck.
facts: It had one of the strongest bites of any land animal ever, strong enough to crunch bone. Its fossil poo is full of bone chips.
A teenage T. rex could gain about 2 kg a day during its growth spurt.
T. rex was more closely related to a chicken than to a Triceratops or Stegosaurus.

nodes.name: Compsognathus
nodes.summary: A chicken-sized Jurassic hunter, about 1 metre long including its tail, that chased lizards across islands in what is now Germany.
facts: For decades it was the smallest dinosaur known.
One skeleton has a whole lizard preserved in its stomach.
It was found in the same limestone as Archaeopteryx, which looks surprisingly similar.

nodes.name: Sinosauropteryx
nodes.summary: A small, fuzzy hunter from China. Found in 1996, it was the first non-bird dinosaur discovered with feathers.
facts: Pigment cells preserved in its fuzz show it was ginger-brown with a striped tail and a dark 'bandit mask'.
Its feathers were simple hair-like filaments, the earliest stage of feather evolution.

nodes.name: Maniraptorans
nodes.summary: The "hand snatchers": feathered theropods with long arms and a half-moon-shaped wrist bone that let the hand fold sideways. Birds evolved within this group.
facts: That folding wrist later became the wing stroke of flying birds.
Many maniraptorans sat on their nests to brood their eggs, just like birds do.

nodes.name: Therizinosaurus
nodes.summary: A bizarre, pot-bellied, plant-eating theropod from Mongolia with the longest claws of any known animal, up to about 50 cm.
facts: Its claws were first thought to belong to a giant turtle, which is why its name means 'scythe lizard like a turtle'.
Despite its scary claws, it probably used them to pull down branches, not to kill.

nodes.name: Oviraptor
nodes.summary: A toothless, beaked, feathered theropod from Mongolia, wrongly accused for 70 years of stealing eggs.
facts: Its name means 'egg thief': it was found on top of eggs in 1923, and scientists assumed it was raiding a Protoceratops nest.
In the 1990s embryos inside similar eggs proved they belonged to oviraptorids. It was a parent protecting its own nest.
Its relative Citipati has been found sitting on its nest with arms spread over the eggs, exactly like a brooding bird.

nodes.name: Paravians
nodes.summary: Raptors, troodontids and birds: small, big-brained feathered dinosaurs with true wing feathers. Here the line between 'dinosaur' and 'bird' blurs completely.
facts: Anchiornis, from 160 million years ago, was the first dinosaur whose whole colour pattern was worked out: black and white wings with a reddish crest.
Some paravians had long wing feathers on their legs as well as their arms.

nodes.name: Raptors
nodes.summary: Feathered hunters with a big sickle-shaped claw on each foot, held up off the ground to keep it sharp. Their name means 'running lizards'.
facts: They ranged from crow-sized Microraptor to the 6-metre Utahraptor.
Real raptors had feathered arms that looked like wings, not the scaly skin seen in films.

nodes.name: Microraptor
nodes.summary: A crow-sized, four-winged dinosaur from China, with long flight feathers on both its arms and its legs. It could glide, and maybe fly, between trees.
facts: Pigment cells show its feathers were glossy, iridescent black, like a starling's.
Fossils have been found with a bird, a fish, a lizard and a mammal in their stomachs, so it was not a fussy eater.

nodes.name: Deinonychus
nodes.summary: A 3.4-metre raptor with a terrible 12 cm foot claw, whose discovery changed how the world saw dinosaurs.
facts: When John Ostrom described it in 1969, its agile, bird-like build launched the 'Dinosaur Renaissance' and revived the idea that birds are dinosaurs.
The 'Velociraptors' in Jurassic Park were really modelled on Deinonychus.

nodes.name: Velociraptor
nodes.summary: The real Velociraptor was about the size of a turkey, around 2 metres long with its tail and 15 kg, and it was covered in feathers.
facts: Its forearm bones have quill knobs, the bumps where big wing feathers attach in modern birds.
The famous 'Fighting Dinosaurs' fossil shows a Velociraptor kicking its claw into a Protoceratops's neck.

nodes.name: Birds & their earliest kin
nodes.summary: The bird branch of the dinosaur family: every feathered flier closer to today's birds than to Velociraptor, from toothed Jurassic birds to robins.
facts: Many early birds still had teeth, clawed fingers and long bony tails.

nodes.name: Archaeopteryx
nodes.summary: The famous 'first bird': a raven-sized Jurassic flier with feathered wings, but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail. Half dinosaur, half bird.
facts: Its first skeleton was found in 1861, just two years after Darwin's On the Origin of Species: the perfect 'missing link' at the perfect moment.
Only about a dozen skeletons are known, all from the limestone of Solnhofen, Germany.
The British Museum bought the London specimen in 1862 for £700, a fortune at the time.

nodes.name: Confuciusornis
nodes.summary: A crow-sized Cretaceous bird from China and the oldest known bird with a toothless beak.
facts: Thousands of fossils have been found, sometimes dozens on one slab.
Some had a pair of long ribbon-like tail feathers, probably for showing off.
Its wings still had big clawed fingers.

nodes.name: Opposite birds
nodes.summary: The most common birds of the Cretaceous, found on every continent. Most still had teeth and clawed wings, and the whole group vanished with the dinosaurs.
facts: They are named 'opposite birds' because their shoulder bones join the opposite way to those of modern birds.
A hatchling trapped in 99-million-year-old amber shows their chicks hatched with flight feathers, ready to look after themselves.

nodes.name: Hesperornis
nodes.summary: A flightless diving seabird about 1.8 metres long, with teeth and tiny stub wings. It chased fish through the inland sea that covered Kansas.
facts: It swam with its powerful feet, like a giant loon.
Darwin wrote that Othniel Marsh's toothed birds, including Hesperornis, were among the best support for evolution in 20 years.

nodes.name: Ichthyornis
nodes.summary: A tern-sized seabird with a mouth full of teeth, one of the closest relatives of modern birds.
facts: A 3D-preserved skull described in 2018 showed it had both a small beak at the tip of its jaws and teeth behind it.
Its brain was already shaped much like a modern bird's.

nodes.name: Modern birds
nodes.summary: The only dinosaurs to survive the asteroid 66 million years ago. Toothless, beaked and warm-blooded, they have since become about 11,000 species in every habitat on Earth.
facts: Every bird alive, from a hummingbird to an ostrich, is a living dinosaur.
The survivors were probably small, ground-dwelling, seed-eating birds, since forests were wiped out.
There are nearly twice as many bird species as mammal species.

nodes.name: Ratites & tinamous
nodes.summary: The "old jaws": ostriches, emus, rheas, cassowaries, kiwis and the flying tinamous of South America. DNA shows that flightless giants evolved several times independently.
facts: The extinct moa's closest relatives are the flying tinamous of South America, not the other giant birds.
The kiwi's closest relative was the elephant bird of Madagascar, on the other side of the world.

nodes.name: Ostrich
nodes.summary: The largest living bird, up to 2.7 metres tall and 150 kg, sprinting across African savannas on two-toed feet.
facts: It can run at about 70 km/h, faster than any other bird on land.
Its eye is bigger than its brain.
An ostrich egg weighs about as much as 24 chicken eggs.

nodes.name: Emu
nodes.summary: Australia's tallest bird, a shaggy, flightless wanderer that can run at 50 km/h.
facts: In the 1932 'Emu War', Australian soldiers with machine guns failed to stop thousands of emus eating farmers' wheat.
The father sits on the dark-green eggs for about 8 weeks, barely eating or drinking.

nodes.name: Kiwi
nodes.summary: Small, nocturnal, flightless birds from New Zealand with hair-like feathers and nostrils at the very tip of their long beaks, perfect for sniffing out worms.
facts: A kiwi egg can weigh about 20% of its mother's body weight, one of the largest eggs relative to body size of any bird.
The kiwifruit was named after the bird, not the other way round.

nodes.name: Elephant birds
nodes.summary: Gigantic flightless birds of Madagascar, up to 3 metres tall, that died out around 1,000 years ago after people arrived.
facts: Vorombe titan may have weighed over 600 kg, making it the heaviest bird ever known.
Their eggs held about 10 litres, roughly the volume of 150 chicken eggs.
Their closest living relatives are the little kiwis of New Zealand.

nodes.name: Moa
nodes.summary: Nine species of giant flightless birds from New Zealand. The tallest females could reach 3.6 metres with neck stretched. They were hunted to extinction within about 200 years of Polynesian settlers arriving.
facts: Moa had no wings at all, not even tiny bones inside.
Their only predator, apart from people, was Haast's eagle, the largest eagle ever, which disappeared with them.

nodes.name: Neognaths
nodes.summary: The "new jaws": all other modern birds, about 99% of living species, from ducks and chickens to eagles, parrots and songbirds.

nodes.name: Landfowl & waterfowl
nodes.summary: Chickens, turkeys and pheasants plus ducks, geese and swans. This old group was already around before the asteroid struck.
facts: Humans have domesticated more birds from this group than from any other.

nodes.name: Wonderchicken
nodes.summary: The oldest known modern bird: a small, long-legged shorebird with a skull mixing chicken and duck features, which lived less than a million years before the asteroid.
facts: Its skull was hidden inside a small block of rock from a Belgian quarry and only seen with CT scans in 2020.
Scientists nicknamed it the 'Wonderchicken'.

nodes.name: Landfowl
nodes.summary: Chunky, ground-feeding birds that scratch for seeds and burst into short flights: chickens, turkeys, quails, pheasants and peafowl.

nodes.name: Red junglefowl
nodes.summary: A colourful wild bird of South and Southeast Asian forests, and the wild ancestor of every chicken on Earth.
facts: Unlike farm chickens, wild junglefowl are shy, fly well and roost high in trees.
Wild roosters already crow at dawn. Chickens inherited the habit.

nodes.name: Chicken
nodes.summary: The world's most numerous bird: a domesticated red junglefowl, and a living theropod dinosaur in your back garden.
facts: There are over 20 billion chickens alive at any moment, far more than any other bird.
Chickens are living dinosaurs: they share a common ancestor with T. rex and Velociraptor that lived over 160 million years ago.
Early chickens arriving in Europe were often treated as special or sacred birds and buried with people, not eaten.
nodes.origin: Domesticated about 3,500 years ago (c. 1650–1250 BCE) in mainland Southeast Asia, probably central Thailand, mainly from the red junglefowl subspecies Gallus gallus spadiceus. Junglefowl were drawn to the new rice and millet fields of early farmers, and chickens then spread across Asia, Africa and Europe.

nodes.name: Turkey
nodes.summary: A big North American landfowl with a bare, colourful head. Wild turkeys roost in trees, and they were domesticated in Mexico about 2,000 years ago.
facts: Turkeys were domesticated twice: in southern Mexico, and separately by Ancestral Puebloans in the American Southwest.
Despite their weight, wild turkeys can fly in short bursts and run at about 40 km/h.
Benjamin Franklin praised the turkey as 'a bird of courage', but he never really proposed it as America's national bird.

nodes.name: Waterfowl
nodes.summary: Ducks, geese, swans and the odd screamers: water birds with webbed feet and flat, filter-edged bills.
facts: Vegavis, a duck relative from Antarctica, lived right before the asteroid, so ducks shared the world with T. rex.
Its fossil voice box shows it may have honked like a goose.

nodes.name: Mallard
nodes.summary: The classic green-headed duck of ponds across the Northern Hemisphere, and ancestor of nearly all domestic ducks.
facts: Only female mallards make the loud, classic 'quack'.
Almost every domestic duck breed, from Pekin ducks to Indian Runners, descends from the mallard; the Muscovy duck is the only exception.
The drake's green head isn't green pigment. Its colour comes from light bouncing off tiny structures in the feathers.

nodes.name: Geese
nodes.summary: Big grazing waterfowl famous for long migrations in V-formation and loud honking.
facts: Flying in a V saves energy: each goose rides the updraft from the wingtip of the bird ahead.
Bar-headed geese migrate over the Himalayas, climbing to over 6,000 metres.
Domestic geese descend from the greylag goose in Europe and the swan goose in China.

nodes.name: Neoaves
nodes.summary: About 95% of living birds: pigeons, penguins, owls, eagles, parrots, songbirds and many more. Most of their main branches split in an explosion of evolution just after the asteroid.
facts: The branches split so fast that it took the genomes of hundreds of bird species to work out their family tree.

nodes.name: Pigeons & doves
nodes.summary: Plump, seed- and fruit-eating birds found almost everywhere. There is no scientific difference between a 'pigeon' and a 'dove'.
facts: Both parents feed their chicks 'crop milk', a rich liquid made in the throat, something only a few birds can do.
Unlike most birds, pigeons can suck up water like a straw instead of tipping their heads back.

nodes.name: Dodo
nodes.summary: A giant flightless pigeon about 1 metre tall from the island of Mauritius. It vanished less than a century after sailors arrived, and became the symbol of extinction.
facts: Its closest living relative is the jewel-coloured Nicobar pigeon.
Rats, pigs and monkeys brought by ships, which ate its ground-nest eggs, probably did more damage than hungry sailors.
The last widely accepted sighting was in 1662, but it may have hung on until about 1681.

nodes.name: Rock dove
nodes.summary: A wild pigeon of sea cliffs and rocky gorges from Europe to Asia and North Africa. City pigeons are its feral descendants, treating buildings as cliffs.
facts: Pigeons can find their way home from hundreds of kilometres away, using the Sun, Earth's magnetic field and maybe even smell.
They can see ultraviolet light.

nodes.name: Domestic pigeon
nodes.summary: The rock dove tamed: raised for food, for carrying messages and for show, in hundreds of fancy breeds.
facts: Charles Darwin bred pigeons himself and used them in On the Origin of Species to show how much selection can change an animal.
In 1918 a homing pigeon named Cher Ami delivered a message that helped save nearly 200 trapped American soldiers.
nodes.origin: Domesticated from the wild rock dove in the Middle East and Mediterranean at least 5,000 years ago; Mesopotamian tablets and Egyptian art show pigeons kept for food and messages, and some researchers think it began even earlier.

nodes.name: Hummingbirds
nodes.summary: Tiny, jewel-coloured nectar drinkers of the Americas that hover in place by beating their wings in a figure-of-eight, dozens of times a second.
facts: They are the only birds that can fly backwards for long.
The bee hummingbird of Cuba weighs about 2 grams, the smallest bird in the world.
The oldest hummingbird fossils come from Germany, although today they live only in the Americas.

nodes.name: Penguins
nodes.summary: Flightless seabirds of the Southern Hemisphere that 'fly' underwater with stiff flipper-wings. They gave up flight within a few million years of the asteroid.
facts: Emperor penguins can dive over 500 metres deep and hold their breath for more than 25 minutes.
Kumimanu, a penguin from 57 million years ago in New Zealand, may have weighed about 150 kg.
The Galápagos penguin sometimes swims north of the equator, the only penguin that does.

nodes.name: Owls
nodes.summary: Silent night hunters with forward-facing eyes, super-sensitive hearing and soft, fringed feathers that hush their flight.
facts: Owls can't move their eyes, so they turn their heads, up to about 270 degrees.
Barn owls have one ear higher than the other, which lets them pinpoint a mouse in total darkness.

nodes.name: Eagles, hawks & vultures
nodes.summary: Daytime birds of prey with hooked beaks, gripping talons and eyesight far sharper than ours.
facts: Golden eagles can spot a rabbit from about 3 km away.
New Zealand's extinct Haast's eagle, the largest eagle ever, hunted moa many times its own weight.

nodes.name: Bald eagle
nodes.summary: A huge fish-eating eagle of North America and the national bird of the United States. It is not bald: 'bald' once meant white-headed.
facts: One bald eagle nest in Florida was 2.9 metres wide and weighed about 2 tonnes.
Poisoned by the pesticide DDT, it fell to under 500 nesting pairs in the lower 48 states in 1963. Today there are over 300,000 birds.
Movies often dub its weak, chirpy call with the scream of a red-tailed hawk.

nodes.name: Australaves
nodes.summary: A surprising family revealed by DNA: falcons, parrots, songbirds and the seriemas, the last living relatives of the terror birds, all share one common ancestor.
facts: Falcons look like hawks but are much closer to parrots. Their hooked beaks evolved separately.

nodes.name: Terror birds
nodes.summary: Giant flightless predators that ruled South America for tens of millions of years after the dinosaurs died, chasing prey on long legs and killing with hatchet-like beaks.
facts: Kelenken had a skull about 71 cm long, the largest of any known bird.
Their closest living relatives are the seriemas, long-legged South American birds that smash prey against rocks.

nodes.name: Titanis
nodes.summary: The only terror bird known from North America: a flightless predator up to about 2 metres tall that stalked Florida and Texas.
facts: It reached North America from the south around 5 million years ago, one of the first animals in the Great American Interchange.
It probably weighed about 150 kg.

nodes.name: Falcons
nodes.summary: Fast, pointed-winged birds of prey. They look like hawks, but DNA shows they are closer cousins of parrots and songbirds.
facts: Falcons have a notch on their beak, a 'tomial tooth', which they use to break the neck of their prey.

nodes.name: Peregrine falcon
nodes.summary: The fastest animal on Earth: in a hunting dive it can top 380 km/h. It lives on every continent except Antarctica.
facts: The fastest dive ever measured was about 389 km/h.
Many now nest on skyscrapers and hunt city pigeons.

nodes.name: Parrots
nodes.summary: Clever, colourful birds with curved beaks and feet with two toes forward and two back. About 400 species live mostly in the tropics.
facts: Alex, an African grey parrot, learned over 100 words and could name colours, shapes and numbers.
The kākāpō of New Zealand is a flightless, nocturnal parrot and the heaviest in the world.
Some of the oldest parrot fossils come from Europe, including Denmark.

nodes.name: Perching birds
nodes.summary: Sparrows, robins, finches, crows and thousands more: more than half of all bird species. They began in ancient Australia.
facts: Songbirds learn their songs from adults in much the same way babies learn to talk.
Australia's lyrebird can imitate almost any sound, from other birds to camera shutters and chainsaws.

nodes.name: Crows & ravens
nodes.summary: Crows, ravens, jays and magpies: the brainiest birds, which solve puzzles, make tools and plan ahead.
facts: New Caledonian crows bend twigs into hooks to fish insects out of holes.
Crows can recognise individual human faces and remember people who treated them badly for years.
Magpies can recognise themselves in a mirror.
